manifest.sample:
# Starter crate file. Rename the package before you publish it.
[package]
name = "app"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"
rust-version = "1.85"

[dependencies]

toolchain.why: Catches the panic-shaped and intent-shaped mistakes rustc happily compiles - unwrap on a Result, dbg! left in, an assertion softened to a constant, a blanket #[allow] - none of which are type errors.
toolchain.configSample:
avoid-breaking-exported-api = true
allow-unwrap-in-tests = true
allow-expect-in-tests = true
allow-panic-in-tests = true
allow-print-in-tests = true
too-many-arguments-threshold = 7

disallowed-macros = [
    { path = "std::dbg", reason = "debug output must not be committed" },
]

disallowed-methods = [
    { path = "std::env::set_var", reason = "process-global mutation is not thread-safe" },
]
toolchain.wiring: Cargo.toml gains `[lints.clippy]` with `all = { level = "deny", priority = -1 }` plus per-lint entries such as `unwrap_used = "deny"`; workspace members inherit it with `[lints] workspace = true`.

verify.expected: prints `error: used `unwrap()` on a `Result` value` with the seeded file:line and a `-D clippy::unwrap-used` note, and exits 101

toolchain.why: The only check that makes a diff reviewable - it normalises whitespace and import order so a real logic change cannot hide inside a reformat.
toolchain.configSample:
edition = "2021"
max_width = 100
hard_tabs = false
tab_spaces = 4
newline_style = "Unix"
use_small_heuristics = "Default"
use_field_init_shorthand = true
use_try_shorthand = true
reorder_imports = true
reorder_modules = true
merge_derives = true
force_explicit_abi = true
toolchain.wiring: rustfmt.toml at the workspace root is picked up automatically by `cargo fmt`; the gate is `cargo fmt --all --check` run before every other step.

verify.expected: prints a unified diff (`Diff in /path/to/src/lib.rs at line N:`) for each misformatted file and exits 1

toolchain.why: The only step that resolves paths and types - it is what turns an invented import, a hallucinated method or a widened signature into a hard error (E0432, E0433, E0308) rather than a runtime surprise.
toolchain.configSample:
[package]
name = "app"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"
rust-version = "1.85"

[lints.rust]
unsafe_code = "forbid"
unused_must_use = "deny"
unused_results = "warn"
let_underscore_drop = "deny"
missing_docs = "warn"

[lints.clippy]
all = { level = "deny", priority = -1 }
unwrap_used = "deny"
expect_used = "deny"
panic = "deny"
todo = "deny"
unimplemented = "deny"
dbg_macro = "deny"
print_stdout = "deny"
toolchain.wiring: The `[lints.rust]` and `[lints.clippy]` tables above live in Cargo.toml (or `[workspace.lints]` plus `[lints] workspace = true` in each member) so every `cargo check` and `cargo clippy` invocation carries the same levels.

verify.expected: prints `error[E0432]: unresolved import `tokio::runtime::AsyncPool`` (or `error[E0433]: failed to resolve`) and exits 101

toolchain.why: Runs each test in its own process and, unlike `cargo test`, fails the run when nothing matched (`--no-tests fail`) and surfaces SKIPPED counts - this is the step that catches a suite that never actually ran.
toolchain.configSample:
[profile.default]
retries = 0
fail-fast = true
status-level = "fail"
final-status-level = "slow"
slow-timeout = "30s"

[profile.ci]
retries = 0
fail-fast = false
status-level = "skip"
final-status-level = "slow"
failure-output = "immediate-final"
slow-timeout = "60s"
toolchain.wiring: .config/nextest.toml at the workspace root defines the `ci` profile; the project runs it with `cargo nextest run --profile ci`. Doc-tests are not run by nextest, so `cargo test --doc` stays alongside it.
toolchain.ciStep: cargo nextest run --workspace --all-features --profile ci --no-tests fail && cargo test --workspace --doc

verify.expected: a seeded failing test prints a `FAIL [ 0.0xxs] crate test_name` line plus the captured panic and exits 100; an empty suite prints `error: no tests to run` and exits 4

toolchain.why: The only check that reads the resolved dependency graph - RUSTSEC advisories, yanked crates, wildcard version requirements, unknown registries and license drift are invisible to clippy and rustc.
toolchain.configSample:
[advisories]
yanked = "deny"
ignore = []

[licenses]
allow = ["MIT", "Apache-2.0", "BSD-2-Clause", "BSD-3-Clause", "ISC", "Unicode-3.0"]
confidence-threshold = 0.93

[bans]
multiple-versions = "warn"
wildcards = "deny"

[sources]
unknown-registry = "deny"
unknown-git = "deny"
toolchain.wiring: deny.toml at the workspace root (scaffolded by `cargo deny init`) is read automatically by `cargo deny check`; no manifest entry is needed.
toolchain.ciStep: cargo deny check advisories bans licenses sources

verify.expected: prints `error[vulnerability]:` naming the RUSTSEC-YYYY-NNNN id and the affected crate version, and exits 1

seed.sample:
[package]
name = "jig-seed-deny"
version = "0.0.0"
edition = "2021"
publish = false

[dependencies]
time = "=0.1.45"

toolchain.why: Proves Cargo.lock still matches the manifest and that every target actually links - it is what catches a dependency an agent wrote into Cargo.toml but never resolved, or a feature combination that only compiles on the machine it was written on.
toolchain.configSample:
[workspace]
members = ["crates/*"]
resolver = "2"

[workspace.package]
edition = "2021"
rust-version = "1.85"

[workspace.lints.rust]
unsafe_code = "forbid"
unused_must_use = "deny"

[workspace.lints.clippy]
all = { level = "deny", priority = -1 }

[profile.release]
overflow-checks = true
debug = 1
toolchain.wiring: Cargo.lock is committed and every CI invocation passes --locked, so a manifest edit without a matching lockfile update fails the build instead of silently re-resolving.

verify.expected: prints `error: the lock file /path/Cargo.lock needs to be updated but --locked was passed to prevent this` and exits 101

seed.sample:
[package]
name = "jig-seed-lockfile"
version = "0.0.0"
edition = "2021"
publish = false

[dependencies]
libc = "=0.2.155"

classes.title: unwrap/expect on a fallible value in shipping code
agentModes: reaches for .unwrap() to get past a Result the session did not want to thread through the signature
converts a ? into .expect("...") when the enclosing fn does not return Result, rather than changing the return type
leaves .unwrap() in the happy path after a refactor because the test suite only exercises the happy path
classes.gapNotes: The regex cannot tell test code from shipping code, so it fires inside #[cfg(test)] modules where unwrap is idiomatic; clippy.toml allow-unwrap-in-tests/allow-expect-in-tests fixes that for the tool-rule detector only. It also misses the equivalents .unwrap_unchecked(), Option::unwrap_or_else(|| panic!(..)), and slice indexing.

evidence.source: clippy::unwrap_used and clippy::expect_used are listed in the Clippy lint index (rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy, restriction group); allow-unwrap-in-tests / allow-expect-in-tests are documented clippy.toml keys in doc.rust-lang.org/clippy/lint_configuration.html.

classes.title: panic!/todo!/unimplemented! left in a library path
agentModes: stubs a match arm or trait method with todo!() to make the crate compile, then reports the feature as done
writes panic!("unreachable") instead of returning an error variant it would have had to add to the enum
fills an unimplemented branch with unimplemented!() while claiming the module is complete
classes.gapNotes: Misses the panics that arrive through other doors: assert!/assert_eq! in shipping code, Option::expect, integer overflow in debug, and slice indexing. clippy::panic also fires on #[should_panic] test helpers unless allow-panic-in-tests is set.

evidence.source: clippy::panic, clippy::todo and clippy::unimplemented are restriction-group lints in the Clippy lint index (rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy).

classes.title: Result discarded with let _ = or an empty Err arm
agentModes: writes let _ = fallible(); to clear an unused_must_use warning it could not diagnose
adds Err(_) => {} to a match so the code compiles without deciding what the failure means
calls .ok() on a Result purely to drop it, turning a hard failure into a silent no-op
classes.gapNotes: let _ = is genuinely correct for suppressing a lock-guard drop order or an intentionally ignored send on a closed channel, so the driver detector is heuristic and needs a per-repo allowlist. It does not catch .ok(); on its own line, .unwrap_or_default() used to erase an error, or an Err arm that logs and then continues.

evidence.source: clippy::let_underscore_must_use and clippy::unused_result_ok appear in the Clippy lint index; unused_must_use is a warn-by-default rustc lint listed in doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/lints.

classes.title: assertion weakened to make a failing test pass
agentModes: replaces assert_eq!(got, expected) with assert!(got.is_ok()) when the expected value stops matching
drops in assert!(true) so the test body is non-empty after deleting the real check
changes an exact comparison to a range or a truthiness check rather than fixing the code under test
classes.gapNotes: Only catches the two loudest shapes. A softening that changes assert_eq!(got, 42) to assert!(got > 0), widens a float tolerance, or swaps a specific expected error for a catch-all is invisible to both the regex and clippy - only a diff review against the previous assertion catches those.

evidence.source: clippy::assertions_on_constants and clippy::assertions_on_result_states are in the Clippy lint index (rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy).

classes.title: #[ignore] left on a test instead of fixing it
agentModes: adds #[ignore] to a test it cannot make pass, then reports the suite green
marks a test #[ignore = "flaky"] after one non-deterministic failure rather than finding the race
keeps a scaffolding #[ignore] from a debugging loop in the final diff
classes.gapNotes: No lint exists for this - neither clippy nor rustc flags #[ignore], and cargo test / cargo nextest both exit 0 with the test merely counted as ignored, so the check-driver regex is the only gate. The regex deliberately does not fire on #[cfg_attr(miri, ignore)], which means a session can hide a permanent skip behind any cfg_attr predicate.

evidence.source: The #[ignore] test attribute is documented in the Rust book test chapter; the absence of a clippy lint id for it was confirmed against the full Clippy lint index, so no tool-rule detector is claimed.

classes.title: test kept as a name with an empty or trivially-passing body
agentModes: deletes the failing assertions but keeps the #[test] fn so the test count does not drop
replaces a test body with a TODO comment, which leaves an empty block after the comment is stripped
reduces a Result-returning test to a bare Ok(()) so it passes without exercising anything
classes.gapNotes: Only the two degenerate shapes are matched. A test whose body still calls the function but asserts nothing, or one reduced to a single println!, still looks alive to this detector. #[tokio::test] and other custom test attributes are not covered because the attribute path varies per crate; extend the pattern per repo.

evidence.source: Derived from the #[test] attribute form documented in the Rust book; no clippy or rustc lint inspects test-body emptiness, so no tool-rule id is claimed.

classes.title: #[should_panic] without an expected message
agentModes: wraps a test in #[should_panic] so any panic - including an unrelated unwrap in the setup - counts as a pass
strips the expected = "..." argument when the message drifts, instead of updating it
classes.gapNotes: An expected = "..." substring that is too short or too generic ("error", "failed") passes both the regex and the lint while still accepting the wrong panic. Neither detector checks that the panic came from the line under test rather than from setup code.

evidence.source: clippy::should_panic_without_expect is listed in the Clippy lint index (pedantic group).

classes.title: blanket #[allow] used to silence a diagnostic
agentModes: adds #![allow(dead_code)] at the crate root rather than deleting or wiring up the unused item
annotates a function with #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)] instead of handling the Result
reaches for #[allow(warnings)] when a refactor produces warnings it does not want to triage
classes.gapNotes: The regex only knows the enumerated rustc lint names plus any single clippy:: lint without a reason; #[allow(some_other_lint)] and multi-lint allow lists such as #[allow(dead_code, unused)] slip past it. clippy::allow_attributes_without_reason is a restriction lint and must be enabled explicitly; it accepts any reason string, however hollow.

evidence.source: clippy::allow_attributes and clippy::allow_attributes_without_reason are in the Clippy lint index; the #[expect(..., reason = ...)] form is the stable rustc alternative documented in the rustc lint-levels reference.

classes.title: unsafe used without a safety argument
agentModes: adds unsafe impl Send/Sync for a type holding a raw pointer to get past a "cannot be sent between threads" error
wraps a borrow-checker conflict in an unsafe block with no SAFETY comment explaining the invariant
classes.gapNotes: A SAFETY comment counts as documentation if it appears anywhere in the 300 characters before the unsafe, so a comment attached to the previous item can silence the one after it, and a SAFETY comment longer than 300 characters no longer reaches the code it explains. The word is all that is checked - a SAFETY comment that says nothing (`// SAFETY: trust me`) satisfies both the regex and clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks. `unsafe fn` declarations are not covered here: the Rust convention for those is a `# Safety` doc section, which is clippy::missing_safety_doc's job. `unsafe impl` of a trait other than Send or Sync is deliberately not matched, because those are ordinary trait impls with a marker obligation the regex cannot read. clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks is restriction-group and must be enabled explicitly.

evidence.source: clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks and clippy::not_unsafe_ptr_arg_deref are in the Clippy lint index; unsafe_code is an allow-by-default rustc lint in doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/lints/listing/allowed-by-default.html and is settable to "forbid" from Cargo.toml [lints.rust].

classes.title: `as` cast used to make the types line up
agentModes: appends `as usize` or `as u32` to a mismatched-type error instead of using TryFrom and handling the failure
casts an i64 to f64 to reuse a float helper, silently losing precision on large inputs
widens a signed value with `as u64` to satisfy an API, turning a negative into a huge positive
classes.gapNotes: Plenty of `as` casts are correct and unavoidable (usize <-> u64 on a known-small value, pointer casts, enum-to-integer), so on most codebases this class must run as a review signal rather than a hard gate. The regex does not see casts written as `as _` with inference, and clippy::cast_possible_truncation is pedantic-group so it is off unless enabled.

evidence.source: clippy::cast_possible_truncation, clippy::cast_sign_loss and clippy::as_conversions are all present in the Clippy lint index (pedantic and restriction groups).

classes.title: import or API path that does not exist
agentModes: writes `use tokio::runtime::AsyncPool;` for a type that was never in the crate, recalled from a plausible-sounding API surface
calls a helper on the wrong crate version - the name existed two majors ago, or exists on a different type
imports from a crate that is not in Cargo.toml at all and never runs cargo check to find out
classes.gapNotes: Tool-rule only on purpose: no regex over source text can know which paths resolve, because that depends on the resolved dependency graph and the enabled feature set. cargo check must run with --all-targets --all-features or an invented path behind a disabled feature stays hidden, and a crate missing from Cargo.toml fails earlier during resolution with a different diagnostic than E0432.

evidence.source: E0432 ("An import was unresolved") and E0433 ("An undeclared crate, module, or type was used") confirmed verbatim from `rustc --explain` on rustc 1.94.1.

classes.title: endpoint, host or port hardcoded instead of read from config
agentModes: pins http://localhost:8080 in the client because that is what the session saw working locally
inlines a bind address rather than threading a config struct through the constructor
hardcodes a value it was asked to make configurable, because the config plumbing was the harder half
classes.gapNotes: Only two literal shapes are matched: an http/https URL and a 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1 host:port. A production hostname without a scheme, an S3 bucket name, a database DSN in a non-URL form, and a magic timeout integer are all invisible - there is no way to tell 30 meaning seconds from 30 meaning anything else. A URL that is assembled from pieces, or built with format!, is not seen either. It runs with stripStrings off because the evidence lives inside the literal, so a bind address in a test fixture fires too - scope the paths to src/ and exclude tests/ per repo. No clippy or rustc lint covers this class at all, so the check driver is the whole of it.

evidence.source: No clippy or rustc lint covers hardcoded endpoints; the full Clippy lint index was searched and none matched, so this class is check-driver only.

classes.title: credential embedded in source
agentModes: pastes a working key into a const so the example it just wrote actually runs
moves a secret out of an env var and into the source when the env lookup returned None during a test run
classes.gapNotes: Name-driven and therefore heuristic: a credential stored in a const called BOOTSTRAP or CFG_BLOB is invisible, and a long non-secret literal named SECRET_HEADER_NAME is a false positive. Strings and comments are both left in, because a key is evidence wherever it sits and a commented-out credential is still a committed credential - the cost is that a long base64 asset or a sample key quoted in a doc comment fires too. The base64 pattern needs 32 unbroken characters, so a key split across concatenated literals or a raw string spanning lines is missed. It reads only .rs files, so a key committed to a .env, a fixture JSON or a CI workflow is out of scope - pair this with a dedicated secret scanner in CI.

evidence.source: No clippy lint detects embedded credentials (the full Clippy lint index was searched); cargo-deny covers dependency supply chain, not source secrets, so no tool-rule id is claimed here.

classes.title: dependency pinned to "*" in Cargo.toml
agentModes: writes version = "*" because it does not know which version has the API it just called
loosens a pin to "*" to make cargo resolve after adding a crate mid-session

fixtures.violation:
[package]
name = "ingest"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
rand = "*"
serde = { version = "*", features = ["derive"] }
fixtures.nearMiss:
[package]
name = "ingest"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"
include = ["src/**/*.rs", "Cargo.toml"]

[dependencies]
rand = "0.8.5"
wildcard = "0.3"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

[dev-dependencies]
proptest = "1"

classes.gapNotes: Fixtures for this class are TOML, not Rust, because the mistake lives in the manifest. Comments are dropped before matching, so a commented-out `# rand = "*"` is ignored until somebody uncomments it. It does not catch the softer versions of the same drift - a `>=1.0` range, a `*` written inside a wider requirement such as `1.*`, a git dependency without a rev, a path dependency pointing outside the workspace, or a wildcard inherited through [workspace.dependencies] in another file. The second pattern matches any `version = "*"`, so a wildcard in a [patch] or [replace] table reads the same as one in [dependencies]. clippy::wildcard_dependencies only fires when the cargo group is enabled (`cargo clippy -- -W clippy::cargo`).

evidence.source: clippy::wildcard_dependencies is listed in the Clippy lint index under the cargo group; the manifest dependency syntax is from doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html.

classes.title: dbg!/println!/eprintln! left in a library path
agentModes: instruments a function with dbg!() while chasing a bug and never removes it
uses println! for progress reporting in a library where the project uses tracing
classes.gapNotes: A binary crate legitimately prints, so scope the paths to library modules or set allow-print-in-tests plus a src/bin exclusion. The regex does not catch print!/eprint! without the newline suffix, std::io::stdout().write_all, or a logging macro configured to write to stdout.

evidence.source: clippy::dbg_macro, clippy::print_stdout and clippy::print_stderr are restriction-group lints in the Clippy lint index; allow-print-in-tests is a documented clippy.toml key.

classes.title: process::exit or abort called outside main
agentModes: calls process::exit(1) on a validation failure instead of returning an error to the caller
aborts on an inconsistent state to avoid designing an error path, which kills the caller and skips destructors
classes.gapNotes: Exiting from main is correct, and this detector cannot tell main from a library module - scope the paths or accept a wave-off on src/main.rs. clippy::exit covers process::exit only; std::process::abort and libc::_exit are matched by the regex but by no lint.

evidence.source: clippy::exit is a restriction-group lint in the Clippy lint index; no clippy lint for std::process::abort was found in that index, which is why the regex carries that half.

classes.title: floating-point compared with ==
agentModes: writes assert_eq!(mean(..), 0.3) and then softens or deletes the test when it fails by one ULP
compares an accumulated f64 to a literal in business logic rather than against a tolerance
classes.gapNotes: Only literal-shaped comparisons are seen. `a == b` between two f64 variables, `assert_eq!(x, y)` on two computed floats, and comparisons via PartialEq on a struct with float fields all pass the regex - clippy::float_cmp is the detector that actually covers those, and it is a pedantic-group lint that must be enabled. Exponent literals such as 1e-9 are deliberately not matched.

evidence.source: clippy::float_cmp is listed in the Clippy lint index (pedantic group).

classes.title: slice indexed without a bounds check
agentModes: writes parts.get(0).unwrap() after a split, assuming the input always has the shape the sample had
indexes buf[offset + n] from a parsed length field without validating it against the buffer
classes.gapNotes: Catches only two of many shapes: plain v[i], v[i..j] range slicing, HashMap index syntax and s[..n] on a String are all unmatched by the regex. clippy::indexing_slicing covers those but is restriction-group and is noisy on code with genuinely known-good indices, so most repos need it scoped rather than global.

evidence.source: clippy::indexing_slicing and clippy::string_slice are restriction-group lints in the Clippy lint index.

classes.title: arithmetic that can overflow, wrap or divide by zero
agentModes: writes total / count for an average without proving count is non-zero
indexes with items.len() - 1 on a slice that can be empty, which underflows a usize into a huge index
classes.gapNotes: The division half is heuristic - it fires on float division and on integer division that is provably safe, so it is a review signal, not a gate. Addition and multiplication overflow are not matched at all by the regex; that is entirely on clippy::arithmetic_side_effects, which is restriction-group, extremely noisy on arithmetic-heavy crates, and blind to overflow in release builds where the wrap is silent.

evidence.source: clippy::arithmetic_side_effects and clippy::integer_division are restriction-group lints confirmed present in the Clippy lint index.

classes.title: blocking call inside an async fn
agentModes: uses std::thread::sleep inside an async fn because it is the sleep the session remembered
takes a std::sync::Mutex guard with .lock().unwrap() and holds it across an .await, which can deadlock the executor
classes.gapNotes: The regex bridges forward at most 400 characters from the `async fn` header, so it is positional, not scoped: a blocking call declared before the async fn is missed (as in the near-miss), one further than 400 characters into a long body is missed, and a blocking call in a plain fn that happens to follow an async fn is a false positive. Real scoping is clippy::await_holding_lock, which understands the guard lifetime but only covers lock guards, not blocking I/O or sleeps. The near-miss needs tokio in the manifest to compile.

evidence.source: clippy::await_holding_lock (suspicious group) and clippy::unused_async are both present in the Clippy lint index.

classes.title: clone() sprayed to get past the borrow checker
agentModes: adds .clone() at each borrow error until the code compiles, without changing the ownership design
passes &value.clone() where &value would do, allocating for nothing on every call
classes.gapNotes: Only the two most obviously wasteful shapes are matched; the common case - one .clone() per borrow error, each individually defensible - is exactly what the regex cannot judge, which is why the detector is a signal and not a gate. clippy::redundant_clone lives in the nursery group, so it is off by default and known to have false positives; enable it with `-W clippy::nursery` and expect to wave some off.

evidence.source: clippy::redundant_clone (nursery group) and clippy::clone_on_copy are both listed in the Clippy lint index; the nursery group is documented as experimental in doc.rust-lang.org/clippy/lints.html.

classes.title: mem::forget or Box::leak used to dodge a lifetime
agentModes: reaches for Box::leak to manufacture a &'static reference the signature demanded
calls mem::forget on a value whose Drop impl was causing a double-free or a borrow conflict, leaking the resource instead
classes.gapNotes: Box::leak is legitimate for once-per-process configuration, so this class needs a per-repo allowlist rather than a hard block. The regex misses std::mem::forget written with the full path split across lines, ManuallyDrop used to skip a Drop impl, Vec::leak / String::leak, and a leak reached through an alias such as `use std::mem::forget as keep;`. clippy::mem_forget is restriction-group and covers mem::forget only.

evidence.source: clippy::mem_forget is a restriction-group lint in the Clippy lint index; no lint for Box::leak was found there, so the regex carries that half.

classes.title: type erased to dyn Any to silence a type error
agentModes: replaces a typed enum with Box<dyn Any> when two branches would not unify, then downcasts at every read site
widens a struct field to dyn Any rather than adding the variant the design actually needed
classes.gapNotes: No clippy or rustc lint covers this - dyn Any is a legitimate tool for plugin registries and panic payload inspection, and the compiler has no opinion about it - so the check driver is the only detector and it must be waved off wherever erasure is the design. It also does not catch the other widening moves: swapping a typed struct for serde_json::Value, a String, or a HashMap<String, String>.

evidence.source: The full Clippy lint index was searched for a dyn Any / downcast lint and none exists; std::any::Any and downcast_ref are documented in the std library reference.

classes.title: Fewer test cases after the edit than before it
agentModes: Deletes the failing test case and reports the suite green
Trims a parameterised case list down to the inputs that already pass
Removes the whole case rather than the assertion inside it, so no empty test body is left to find
classes.gapNotes: A removal is not in any file's content — the deleted case is absent from the file that is left, so the committed check driver reports this class skipped on a normal run and proves it only from the fixture pair, which carries the file before the edit and the file after it. Nothing in this catalogue watches it — a catalogue never carries a session guard — so the class ships as a named mistake with a proven pair and no lane, and the plan grades that cell GAP. The lane is an authored `edit-guard` on the same removal rule, which reads one edit at a time: an Edit payload carries the text it replaced, so a case deleted out of a `mod tests` block is seen, and a Write payload carries none, so a whole-file rewrite that drops a source file is not. Author it to observe: one call cannot see the case being put back two calls later, and a deletion can be right — behaviour that genuinely went away takes its tests with it, which is a judgement no count can make.

evidence.source: No tool in the Rust ecosystem gates on a drop in test count between two revisions; the runners report what they discovered, never what they stopped discovering. The judgement that a shrinking suite is a defect is jig's own.
